Byte stream vs character stream: when do you use each?

Byte streams handle raw data: images, archives, encrypted content. Character streams handle text, and apply a charset to decode. Using a Reader on binary data corrupts it, because invalid byte sequences get replaced. InputStreamReader is the bridge between the two.
Why does InputStream.read() return int rather than byte?

It must represent 256 byte values plus one "end of stream" signal, which is 257 states. A byte has 256. So it returns 0 to 255, or -1. Casting to byte before comparing makes 0xFF look like end of stream: a loop over {1, 0xFF, 2} stopped after one byte in testing.
What is the Decorator pattern in java.io?

Each wrapper implements the same abstract type and holds an instance of it, adding a feature. new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(f)), UTF_8)) stacks four behaviours. Without decorators, you would need a subclass per combination. Closing the outermost closes all.
Why is buffered I/O faster? Does flush guarantee that data is on disk?

A buffer reduces system calls by moving data in blocks. flush only hands bytes to the OS, where they sit in the page cache. Surviving a power failure takes FileChannel.force(true) or FileDescriptor.sync(), and those are slow, so databases group them.
What is the output? var w = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(f)); w.write("hello"); System.out.println(Files.size(path)); w.close(); System.out.println(Files.size(path));
0, then 5. The data stays in the 8 KB buffer until flushed. close flushes first. Without close, the data would be lost on exit.
Why might a text file look fine on one machine and show garbled characters on another?

The bytes were encoded in one charset and decoded in another. Before Java 18, the default charset depended on the platform, so new FileReader(f) differed between Windows (often windows-1252) and Linux (UTF-8). Fix by always naming the charset. Since Java 18, UTF-8 is the default, which can itself change behaviour for old Windows apps; -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT restores the old behaviour.
Predict the output. String s = "héllo"; System.out.println(s.length()); System.out.println(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length); System.out.println(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_16).length);
5, 6, 12. é takes 2 bytes in UTF-8. Java's UTF_16 encoder writes a 2-byte byte order mark, plus 2 bytes for each of 5 chars.
What does String.length() return for an emoji?

2 for most emoji, since it counts UTF-16 code units, and characters above U+FFFF need a surrogate pair. codePointCount returns 1. For user-visible characters (grapheme clusters, like flags), use BreakIterator. substring can split a pair and corrupt the text.
File vs Path: why was NIO.2 added?

File returns booleans on failure with no reason, handles symlinks poorly, lacks attribute support, and loads whole directories. NIO.2's Path and Files (Java 7) throw precise exceptions, stream directories lazily, offer atomic moves, attributes and file systems beyond the default one, such as inside a ZIP.
Predict the results. Path.of("/a/b").resolve("/x"); Path.of("/a/b").relativize(Path.of("/a/c/d")); Path.of("/home/a/../b/./c.txt").normalize(); Path.of("abc").startsWith("a");
/x (an absolute argument replaces the base), ../c/d, /home/b/c.txt, and false: startsWith compares whole path elements, not string prefixes.

What is the role of flip, clear, compact and rewind in ByteBuffer?

flip: switch from filling to draining (limit = position; position = 0). clear: reset for filling, without erasing. compact: keep unread data by moving it to the front. rewind: reread the same content. Example from Java 21: after 3 puts, pos=3 lim=8; after flip, pos=0 lim=3; after one get, pos=1; after compact, pos=2 lim=8.
Direct vs heap buffers?

Heap buffers wrap a byte array on the Java heap, and are cheap to allocate. The OS cannot use movable heap memory directly, so the JVM copies through native memory. Direct buffers live off-heap, skip that copy, and cost more to allocate and free. Use direct, pooled, long-lived buffers for heavy socket or file I/O. They do not count toward -Xmx, but have their own limit, and hasArray() is false.
How does a Selector work? Why must you remove keys from selectedKeys?

Channels in non-blocking mode register interest in events. select() blocks until the OS (epoll or similar) reports readiness and adds keys to the selected set. The selector only adds to the set; it never removes. If you do not remove a handled key, the next loop sees it again, and processes a stale event, such as accept() returning null.
Explain BIO, NIO and AIO. How do virtual threads change the choice?

BIO: one blocking thread per connection, simple but limited by platform thread cost. NIO: a few threads multiplex many non-blocking channels, scalable but with complex code. AIO: the kernel or a pool notifies you on completion; rarely used in Java. Virtual threads make blocking cheap, so one thread per connection scales again, with a simple programming model. For many applications, this removes the reason to use reactive code just for scale. Frameworks like Netty still use NIO directly.
What is zero-copy, and how do you do it in Java?

A normal file-to-socket send copies disk to kernel buffer, to user buffer, to socket buffer. FileChannel.transferTo can use sendfile, so the kernel moves data directly, with no user-space copy and less CPU. Kafka relies on this for consumers. It does not apply if data must be modified in user space, such as with TLS (unless kernel TLS is used).
When are memory-mapped files useful, and what are the pitfalls?

For large random-access files, where the OS page cache does the caching, and access looks like arrays. Pitfalls: 2 GB per buffer, no explicit unmap (Windows then blocks deletion), page faults stall a thread with no timeout, and force is needed for durability. Since Java 22, the FFM API's MemorySegment with an Arena removes the size and unmap limits.
What limitations does WatchService have?

Not recursive; you must reset the key; events can be lost (OVERFLOW); multiple events per save; the implementation varies, polling on some platforms; often no support on network file systems. Make the handler idempotent, and rescan on overflow.
What is the purpose of serialVersionUID? What happens if you omit it?

It is the version identifier compared on deserialization. If omitted, the JVM computes it from the class structure, so harmless edits or a different compiler can change it, causing InvalidClassException on existing data. Declare private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;, and change it only for intentional incompatibility.

Predict the output. Non-serializable parent, serializable child. class Base { int b = 5; Base() { System.out.println("Base()"); b = 9; } } class Child extends Base implements Serializable { int c = 7; transient int t = 8; static int s = 1; Child() { System.out.println("Child()"); } } Child x = new Child(); x.b = 50; x.c = 70; x.t = 80; byte[] data = serialize(x); Child r = (Child) deserialize(data); System.out.println(r.b + " " + r.c + " " + r.t);

Base()
Child()
Base()
9 70 0
new Child() prints both constructors. Deserializing runs only the first non-serializable ancestor's constructor. b is not in the stream, so Base's constructor sets 9. c is restored. t is transient and gets 0: neither the constructor nor the initializer runs for Child.
Are constructors called during deserialization? Do transient final fields work?

Constructors of serializable classes are not called. Only the no-arg constructor of the nearest non-serializable superclass runs. So a transient final field (other than a compile-time constant) comes back as null or zero and cannot be assigned in readObject by normal code. That is one reason to prefer a serialization proxy or records.
How can serialization break a singleton, and how do you stop it?

Deserialization creates a new instance, ignoring the private constructor. Add private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }, and make instance fields transient, or use an enum, which is safe by specification. Verified: without readResolve, the instance differed.
What does the serialization proxy pattern do?

A class's writeReplace returns a small private nested proxy holding the logical state. The proxy's readResolve rebuilds the object through its public constructor or factory, so invariants are checked, and final fields work. The outer class's readObject throws InvalidObjectException, to block forged streams. EnumSet uses it. Records give you the same benefit natively.
Serializable vs Externalizable?

With Serializable, the JVM writes all non-transient fields by reflection, and no constructor of the class runs. With Externalizable, you write and read exactly what you want, and a public no-arg constructor is mandatory, because it runs first. Externalizable gives speed and format control, at the cost of hand-maintained code. Neither fixes the security problem.
Why is Java deserialization dangerous? How do you mitigate it?

Because readObject creates arbitrary classes, and runs their code before the application sees the object. An attacker uses gadget chains in common libraries for remote code execution. Mitigate by not accepting serialized objects from untrusted sources, using JSON or Protobuf, adding ObjectInputFilter allow-lists, and keeping dependencies up to date. Casting the result is no protection, as the damage is already done by then.
What happens with an object written twice to one ObjectOutputStream?

The stream keeps a handle table. The second write stores a back-reference, so identity and cycles are preserved, and later changes to the object are not recorded. Tested: writing v=1, changing to 2, and writing again read back 1 and 1, the same object. out.reset() clears the table. This table also retains every object written, so a long-lived stream leaks memory without reset.
How would you version data if you moved away from Java serialization?

Use JSON with tolerant readers (FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES off), and add fields as optional. Or Protobuf or Avro, where each field has a stable number or the schema is registered. Migrate by writing both formats during transition, then reading the new one first, and falling back on the old.
Why can getProperty return null after put("n", 5)?

getProperty only returns String values, and treats anything else as absent. Properties extends Hashtable<Object, Object>, so put accepts an Integer. Always use setProperty. Verified: getProperty("n") printed null while get("n") printed 5. load(InputStream) also assumes ISO-8859-1.
What is Zip Slip?

A path traversal attack during extraction: entry names with ../ write outside the target folder, potentially replacing executables or configs. Resolve and normalize the name, then check target.startsWith(base). Verified: /tmp/out resolved with ../../etc/passwd normalizes to a path that does not start with the base.
How would you replace a file safely so readers never see partial content?

Write to a temp file in the same directory (same file system), force it to disk if durability matters, then call Files.move(tmp, target, ATOMIC_MOVE, REPLACE_EXISTING). Rename is atomic on POSIX file systems. A move across file systems is a copy, which is why ATOMIC_MOVE then fails with AtomicMoveNotSupportedException.
How do you make a Socket read not hang forever?

Use setSoTimeout(ms) for reads, and connect(addr, timeoutMs) for connecting. The read then throws SocketTimeoutException, and the socket stays usable. Verified with ServerSocket.setSoTimeout(50): accept threw SocketTimeoutException: Accept timed out. Without a timeout, a silently dead peer leaves the thread blocked. In HttpClient, set both connect and request timeouts.
Why is one read not one message on a TCP socket?

TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries. A send may arrive split or merged with others. Define framing: a delimiter like newline, a fixed size, or a length prefix, and loop until the frame is complete. DataInputStream.readFully helps with that.
HttpClient vs HttpURLConnection vs RestTemplate vs WebClient vs RestClient?

HttpURLConnection is the old JDK API: clumsy, no HTTP/2. java.net.http.HttpClient (Java 11) is modern, supports HTTP/2 and async, and has no JSON mapping. In Spring, RestTemplate is the older synchronous client; WebClient is reactive; RestClient (Spring 6.1) is the modern synchronous fluent API. In Spring apps, use RestClient or WebClient, and set timeouts. A client should be a shared bean, to reuse connections.
Does HttpClient.send throw on a 500 response? What are the defaults worth changing?

No. It returns a response with status 500; only transport problems throw (IOException, HttpTimeoutException). Defaults to revisit: no redirects followed, no connect or request timeout. Reuse a single client, as creating many leaks threads and connections until collected.
Why does URL make a bad map key?

URL.equals and hashCode resolve host names, which blocks on DNS, and gives results that vary with the network. Two hosts with one IP compare equal. Use URI, whose equals is purely textual (scheme and host case-insensitive, per its rules).
Why is the password from Console.readPassword a char[]?

Strings are immutable, and may be retained in the heap or string pool, appearing in heap dumps. A char[] can be wiped by your code straight after use. The same applies to JPasswordField.getPassword. Note that System.console() may be null in IDEs or when input is redirected, particularly before Java 22.
Scenario: an app slowly hits "Too many open files". How do you find and fix it?

- Confirm it: lsof -p <pid>, group by path or type, and compare to ulimit -n.
- Look for unclosed items: Files.lines/Files.list without TWR, responses or sockets not closed, a new HttpClient per request.
- Fix with try-with-resources, and share clients.
- Only raise the limit after fixing leaks, if real load demands it.
- Add a metric for open file descriptors; JVM metrics expose this via Micrometer.
Scenario: upload a 5 GB file through a Spring service. How do you avoid running out of memory?

Do not buffer it in a byte[] or a MultipartFile.getBytes() call. Stream it: read from getInputStream() and use transferTo to a Path or object storage, in fixed-size chunks. Enforce size limits, validate the type, generate server-side names to avoid traversal, and hold no transaction during the copy. For very large files, give clients a pre-signed URL to upload straight to storage, with multipart resume.
Design question: build a simple log tailer that ships new lines from a growing file.

- Keep the last offset in a state file, so a restart resumes.
- Open the file with FileChannel or RandomAccessFile, seek to the offset, read until end, and handle a partial last line by waiting for its newline.
- Use WatchService as a hint, with polling as a fallback, since events can be lost.
- Detect rotation: file size smaller than the offset, or a changed file key (BasicFileAttributes.fileKey()).
- Ship in batches, and advance the offset only after success, for at-least-once delivery.
How do you call a method that throws IOException inside a stream's map()?

Catch it inside the lambda and rethrow as UncheckedIOException, then catch that outside the pipeline and unwrap with getCause() if callers expect a checked exception. Alternatives: a small helper/functional interface that throws, or a plain loop. Don't swallow it or wrap it in a bare RuntimeException that loses the type.
A user uploads a file named "../../etc/cron.d/x". How do you store uploads safely?

Never use the client's file name as a path. Generate your own name (e.g. a UUID) and keep the original name only as metadata. If you must use it, take Path.of(name).getFileName(), then base.resolve(it).normalize() and verify startsWith(base). Also check size limits, validate the content type by inspecting bytes rather than trusting the extension or header, and store outside the web root.
What is Base64 and when do you use it? Which encoder?

Base64 turns arbitrary bytes into ASCII text (about 33% larger) so binary data can travel in JSON, headers, URLs or emails. It is encoding, not encryption. java.util.Base64.getEncoder() is the standard alphabet, getUrlEncoder() uses - and _ (used by JWT, often with withoutPadding()), and getMimeEncoder() adds line breaks. For large files use encoder.wrap(outputStream) to stream instead of building a huge string.
How do you parse a 3 GB JSON array without running out of memory?

Use Jackson's streaming API: create a JsonParser, advance to START_ARRAY, then bind each element with mapper.readValue(parser, Item.class) (or readerFor(Item.class).readValues(…) for a MappingIterator) and process it before moving on. Memory is bounded by one record. Combine with batching for DB inserts. Better still, ask producers for NDJSON (one JSON object per line), which is trivially streamable and splittable.
Two instances of a scheduled job run on the same server. How do you make sure only one processes the file?

On one machine, take an exclusive FileChannel.tryLock() on a lock file and exit if it returns null; the OS releases it if the process dies. Remember it is JVM-wide and often advisory. Across several machines this does not work reliably, so use a DB lock row, ShedLock, or move the file atomically to a "processing" folder (ATOMIC_MOVE) so only the instance whose move succeeds owns it.
